title: Build Systems, CMake and Toolchains
objectives: Describe the pipeline from preprocessor to compiler to linker, and what each stage consumes and produces
Explain what a build system adds over manual compilation: dependency graph, incremental builds, parallelism, portability
Write a CMakeLists.txt using target-based commands (add_library, add_executable, target_link_libraries) with out-of-source builds
Configure build types and flags (Debug vs Release, warnings, sanitizers) and explain why Debug-only bugs appear in CI Release builds
motivation: A pricing library of 400 source files cannot be compiled by hand, and more importantly, when one header changes, recompiling all 400 files wastes minutes on every developer, dozens of times a day. Build systems turn 'what depends on what' into a graph and rebuild exactly the minimum. For a C++ trading desk there is a second reason: the flags the build passes to the compiler (optimisation, warnings, sanitizers) determine both the speed of the binaries that trade and the bugs that escape to production.

blocks.md: A C++ translation unit goes through three tools. The **preprocessor** handles `#include` and macros, producing one big translation unit, which is why headers must contain declarations, not definitions, or you get duplicate-symbol errors at link time. The **compiler** translates each unit to an **object file** (`.o`): machine code for that file's functions plus a symbol table of what it defines and what it still needs. The **linker** stitches object files and libraries together, resolving every referenced symbol against some definition; an unresolved symbol is the classic `undefined reference to ...` error. **Separate compilation** is the performance win: after editing `fills.cpp`, only `fills.o` recompiles and the link step re-runs, not every file.

blocks.code:
g++ -E main.cpp  > /dev/null   # preprocess only: see what #include expands to
g++ -S main.cpp                # compile to assembly (main.s)
g++ -c main.cpp                # compile to object file (main.o)
g++ -c fills.cpp               # separate compilation: one unit at a time
g++ main.o fills.o -o trading_app   # link: resolve symbols into the executable
blocks.caption: The stages exist as separate tools; a build system automates running exactly the stale ones.

blocks.text: Why a build system at all

blocks.md: Typing `g++` by hand fails at team scale for four reasons. A **dependency graph** must be tracked: which headers does each file include, so the build knows what is stale? **Incremental builds** must skip everything up to date, the difference between 30-second and 10-minute feedback loops. **Parallelism** must compile independent units at once (`-j`), since a 16-core machine should not compile serially. And **portability** must hide the differences between Linux, macOS and CI images. Build systems do this bookkeeping; CMake additionally is a **generator**: it writes the actual build files (Makefiles or Ninja) for the platform, so one CMakeLists.txt drives all of them.

Modern CMake is **target-based**: you declare targets (libraries, executables, tests) and attach include directories, compile options and dependencies to each target, not to the whole project. A library that publishes its include directory via `PUBLIC` propagates it to everything that links it, the caller never hand-lists header paths. Builds are **out-of-source**: all generated files land in a build directory, so `git status` stays clean and deleting the directory is a full clean.

blocks.code:
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.16)
project(trading_app LANGUAGES CXX)

set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)

add_library(fills STATIC src/fills.cpp)          # static library target
target_include_directories(fills PUBLIC include)  # propagate headers to consumers
target_compile_options(fills PRIVATE -Wall -Wextra -Werror)

add_executable(trading_app src/main.cpp)         # executable target
target_link_libraries(trading_app PRIVATE fills) # pulls in headers + lib automatically

enable_testing()
add_executable(fills_test tests/fills_test.cpp)
target_link_libraries(fills_test PRIVATE fills)
add_test(NAME fills_test COMMAND fills_test)     # discovered by ctest
blocks.caption: One CMakeLists.txt: library, application and tests, with warnings enforced on the library only.

blocks.code:
cmake -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release   # configure (out-of-source)
cmake --build build -j 8                    # compile+link in parallel
cd build && ctest                           # run the test suite
blocks.caption: Configure once, then build/test; CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE selects the flag set.

blocks.text: Toolchains and flags: where bugs hide

blocks.md: The **build type** is a flag bundle: Debug typically `-g -O0` (symbols, no optimisation, fast compile) and Release `-O2/-O3 -DNDEBUG` (optimised, asserts compiled out). This explains a classic CI failure: code that works in Debug and crashes in Release usually relies on **undefined behaviour** the optimiser rearranged, an uninitialised variable or an out-of-bounds read that 'happened' to be harmless at `-O0`. The defenses are mechanical: treat warnings as errors (`-Werror`) so new problems cannot accumulate, and run **sanitizers** in one CI build (`-fsanitize=address,undefined` in a Debug-type build) to make UB crash loudly. Deterministic, reproducible builds, pinned compiler versions and flags, matter extra in finance, where you must be able to rebuild the exact binary that traded.

blocks.title: Stale artefacts and committed builds
blocks.md: Two hygiene rules. First, never commit build outputs: `build/` belongs in .gitignore, and binaries in a repository make history enormous and reviews meaningless. Second, when builds behave inexplicably, phantom 'undefined reference' after renaming a header, suspect a stale build directory and reconfigure from scratch; incremental builds are only as correct as their dependency data.

guidedExercise.prompt: Write the CMakeLists.txt for a project with a static library `risk` (sources in `src/`, public headers in `include/`), a test executable `risk_test` from `tests/risk_test.cpp`, C++17 enforced, warnings-as-errors on the library, and the tests registered with ctest. Then give the three commands to configure, build and test it from the project root.
hints: STATIC keyword on add_library; PUBLIC include directory so the test sees the headers.
enable_testing() + add_test(); run with ctest inside the build dir.
guidedExercise.solution:
```cmake
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.16)
project(risk_engine LANGUAGES CXX)

set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)

add_library(risk STATIC src/risk.cpp)
target_include_directories(risk PUBLIC include)
target_compile_options(risk PRIVATE -Wall -Wextra -Werror)

enable_testing()
add_executable(risk_test tests/risk_test.cpp)
target_link_libraries(risk_test PRIVATE risk)
add_test(NAME risk_test COMMAND risk_test)
```

```bash
cmake -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug
cmake --build build -j
cd build && ctest
```

Because the include directory is PUBLIC on `risk`, the test target inherits it through `target_link_libraries` - no manual `-I include` anywhere.

independentExercise.prompt: A developer's build passes locally (Debug) but the CI Release build crashes in the position-update path with garbage numbers. (a) Name the most likely class of bug and why Debug hides it. (b) Give the compile-flag changes that make CI catch it mechanically, and the one-line code smell to hunt first.
hints: Debug = -O0 -g; Release = -O2 -DNDEBUG, the optimiser reorders code that the standard calls undefined.
Sanitizers turn undefined behaviour into a loud crash instead of silent garbage.
An uninitialised double read before first write is the classic.
independentExercise.solution:
(a) Most likely **undefined behaviour**, typically reading an uninitialised variable (or an out-of-bounds access) that happens to read benign memory at `-O0`. At `-O2` the optimiser assumes UB never happens, reorders/eliminates code accordingly, and the garbage becomes visible. It is not 'the optimiser's bug', the source violated the contract.

(b) Mechanical defences:

```cmake
target_compile_options(risk PRIVATE -Wall -Wextra -Werror)
# plus a sanitizer build target in CI:
target_compile_options(risk_sanitized PRIVATE -fsanitize=address,undefined -g)
target_link_options(risk_sanitized PRIVATE -fsanitize=address,undefined)
```

Warnings-as-errors stops new suspicious code at review; the sanitizer build crashes loudly with a stack trace instead of producing wrong numbers. The first thing to hunt: a `double` (e.g. `avg_cost`) declared without an initialiser and read before every path assigns it.

commonMistakes: Putting definitions in headers so multiple translation units each define the same symbol, duplicate-symbol link errors.
Committing build/ directories or binaries into the repository.
Debugging a Release failure with Debug reasoning: -O2 plus -DNDEBUG (asserts removed) changes program behaviour only when the code relied on undefined behaviour.
Adding include directories globally with include_directories() instead of per-target PUBLIC/PRIVATE propagation.
Assuming an incremental build is correct after moving/renaming files, when in doubt, reconfigure a fresh build directory.
realWorldApplication: Every C++ shop on a trading floor runs CMake (or Bazel) driving Ninja/Make, with CI matrix builds across compilers; reproducible Release binaries are an audit requirement because you must be able to rebuild the exact code that executed a trade.
quantFinanceApplication: Latency-critical paths are built Release with profile-guided optimisation and checked with sanitizers in parallel CI builds; the Debug-passes-Release-crashes pattern here is a daily reality in low-latency C++ teams.
summary: Pipeline: preprocessor (headers/macros) -> compiler (per-unit object files with symbol tables) -> linker (resolves symbols into the binary).
Build systems track the dependency graph, rebuild only stale units, parallelise and hide platform differences; CMake generates the platform build files.
Modern CMake is target-based: add_library/add_executable plus target_link_libraries with PUBLIC/PRIVATE propagation; builds are out-of-source.
Debug (-g -O0) vs Release (-O2 -DNDEBUG) explains Debug-only-passing bugs: they are usually undefined behaviour, found with -Werror and sanitizers.
Never commit build artefacts; keep one canonical build configuration in version control so any machine rebuilds the same binary.

options: Combines object files and libraries, resolving every referenced symbol to a definition
quiz.explanation: The linker stitches .o files and libraries into one binary and resolves symbol references; an unresolved reference is the 'undefined reference to ...' error. Expanding includes is the preprocessor's job.

options: A build-system GENERATOR that produces platform build files (Make/Ninja) from declarative CMakeLists.txt
quiz.explanation: CMake does not compile anything itself, it generates the files that drive the actual build tools, which is what makes one CMakeLists.txt portable across platforms.

quiz.prompt: A project has 5 .cpp files, each compiled separately. How many object files does a full (non-incremental) build produce?
quiz.explanation: One .o per translation unit, 5 object files, then a single link step combines them into the executable.

quiz.prompt: State the main trade-off between static and dynamic linking.
quiz.modelAnswer: Static linking copies library code into the executable: self-contained, fast startup, no runtime dependency, but larger binaries and fixes require relinking. Dynamic linking loads shared libraries at runtime: smaller binaries, libraries updated independently, but a runtime dependency that can break if versions mismatch.
quiz.explanation: Static = size and rebuild-on-fix; dynamic = deployment flexibility with version-mismatch risk. Trading infrastructure often static-links for deployment determinism.

quiz.prompt: Which are genuine benefits of out-of-source builds (all outputs under build/)?
options: Source tree stays clean, so git status shows only real changes
A full clean is just deleting one directory
Multiple build types (Debug/Release) can coexist side by side
Compilation becomes faster than in-source builds
quiz.explanation: Out-of-source is about hygiene and parallel configurations, not compile speed. Artefact separation means clean diffs, trivial cleans, and a Debug and Release tree from the same sources.

quiz.prompt: A team's Release build passes `-DNDEBUG`. What is the consequence for the code?
options: assert() checks are compiled out entirely
No consequences. NDEBUG affects only linker output
quiz.explanation: NDEBUG disables the standard assert macro, which is why invariant checks that must always run should not rely on assert, and why Debug-vs-Release behaviour can legitimately differ.

flashcards.front: Three stages of building one translation unit
flashcards.back: Preprocess (#include, macros) -> compile (to object file: machine code + symbols) -> link (resolve symbols across units into the binary).
Compiler output for one translation unit: machine code for its functions plus a symbol table of definitions and undefined references.

flashcards.front: Why Debug passes and Release fails
flashcards.back: Undefined behaviour (uninitialised reads, out-of-bounds) happens to be harmless at -O0 but the -O2 optimiser assumes it away. Defences: -Werror, sanitizers.
All generated files go to a separate build directory: clean git status, trivial full cleans, side-by-side Debug/Release trees.
